prompt: For Calvin Klein: Show our top five products by revenue and, separately, by distinct customers in Q1 2026. Use two compact tables.
follow_up: Which products appear in both rankings? Explain what this suggests about revenue versus customer reach in one short paragraph, without a table.
intent: Rank different product metrics and interpret the actual selected lists without inventing price or volume explanations.
checks: Both: Use Calvin Klein scope and Q1 2026 qualifying sales; revenue sums sale_price and customer counts are distinct user IDs.
Initial: Return five eligible products per ranking when available; handle boundary ties consistently, with compact presentation and no unnecessary evidence dump.
Follow-up: Compare product IDs from the two previously displayed lists; preserve their membership and tie selection.

Follow-up: Use one short prose paragraph; ranking membership alone must not establish higher prices, lower unit volumes, customer motives, or causes. Additional measured evidence may justify narrower descriptive comparisons.

prompt: For Calvin Klein: Compare our Q1 2026 performance with Q4 2025. Show revenue, distinct customers, distinct orders, and average order value, including percentage changes.
follow_up: Can we say that customer acquisition caused the revenue change? Give me a short explanation.
intent: Distinguish observed quarterly arithmetic from unsupported acquisition and causal claims.
checks: Both: Apply the same qualifying-sales rule and requested brand filter to both complete UTC quarters.
Initial: Compute AOV as scoped revenue divided by distinct scoped orders; percentage changes use Q4 as the denominator and handle zero denominators explicitly.
Follow-up: A change in active distinct customers does not establish acquisition; first scoped purchase requires full qualifying history.
Follow-up: Even a measured acquisition change alone does not establish causation. State the evidentiary limit or separate an arithmetic contribution from a causal explanation.

prompt: For Calvin Klein: Which three product categories contributed the most to our revenue change from Q4 2025 to Q1 2026? Rank by the size of the change, keep the signs, and group the rest as Other so everything reconciles.
follow_up: Now make it an executive summary: mention only the two biggest category changes and combine every remaining category into Other. Include the signed amounts and total change in at most three sentences.
intent: Recalculate the remainder after changing the displayed category population.
checks: Both: Use category-level qualifying revenue differences, including categories appearing in only one quarter; rank by absolute change while preserving signs.
Initial: The three displayed changes plus Other must equal the whole-brand revenue change.
Follow-up: Preserve the top two selected categories and recompute Other to include the formerly third category plus all remaining categories.
Follow-up: Show the two signed contributions, revised Other, and total in at most three sentences without an unexplained percentage or causal assertion.

prompt: For Calvin Klein: For our five highest-revenue products in Q1 2026, show revenue, units sold, and average realized selling price per unit.
follow_up: For those same five products, show distinct orders and revenue per order. Explain briefly why that measure can differ from the unit selling price.
intent: Keep item, product-within-order, and whole-brand order grains distinct across a follow-up.
checks: Initial: Rank by qualifying product revenue; units are qualifying item rows and realized unit price is product revenue divided by units.
Follow-up: Preserve the previously selected five products and count distinct orders containing each product.
Follow-up: Divide each product's revenue by its distinct orders; do not silently include other products' revenue or describe it as full-basket AOV.
Both: Explain differences using actual grain and observed quantities; do not infer premium positioning or purchasing motives.

prompt: For Calvin Klein: How many customers placed at least two qualifying orders with us in Q1 2026, and what percentage of our purchasing customers does that represent?
follow_up: Compare the average revenue per customer for those repeat-order customers with customers who placed exactly one qualifying order. Show each group's customer count and revenue too.
intent: Measure repeat ordering and compare mutually exclusive customer cohorts at a consistent grain.
checks: Initial: Define repetition by distinct scoped order IDs within Q1, not multiple items or lifetime purchases.
Initial: Divide customers with at least two qualifying Q1 orders by all customers with at least one qualifying Q1 order.
Follow-up: Preserve the same Q1 cohorts; each customer belongs to exactly one group and group revenue includes their qualifying scoped Q1 items.
Follow-up: Report both customer counts, both revenues, and revenue per customer; an empty cohort has undefined average rather than an invented zero or omitted group.

prompt: For Calvin Klein: How many Q1 2026 customers were buying from our brand for the first time, versus returning customers? Show the revenue from each group.
follow_up: Can I label that first group as customers who were new to the company? Explain the distinction in two sentences.
intent: Use complete authorized purchase history and preserve the difference between brand acquisition and company acquisition.
checks: Initial: Determine first qualifying brand purchase using history before Q1 as well as Q1; do not classify every Q1 customer as new by filtering history too early.
Initial: New means first qualifying scoped purchase in Q1; returning means a qualifying scoped purchase before Q1. Counts and Q1 revenues must reconcile to Q1 totals.
Follow-up: Explain that first purchase from Calvin Klein does not establish first purchase from the company; other-brand history is outside the workspace's scope.
Follow-up: Use two sentences and do not access unauthorized brand history.

prompt: For Calvin Klein: Show our monthly revenue, distinct orders, and distinct customers for January, February, and March 2026 in one table.
follow_up: Add a Q1 total row. Can I get the customer total by adding the three monthly customer counts?
intent: Handle non-additive distinct counts when consolidating monthly metrics.
checks: Initial: Use complete UTC calendar months, consistent qualifying purchases, and display all three months even if one is empty.
Follow-up: Recompute quarter-level distinct customers and orders from the union of qualifying rows rather than assuming monthly distinct counts are additive.
Follow-up: Explain that cross-month customers are counted once in Q1; the numerical sum may coincide only when there is no overlap.
Both: Revenue aggregates must reconcile between monthly rows and Q1.

prompt: For Calvin Klein: Show our Q1 2026 qualifying revenue, then compare it with the item sale-price total when cancelled and returned orders and items are included.
follow_up: How much value is excluded by the qualifying-sales rule, and what percentage of the all-status total is that? Can we call that our refund rate?
intent: Apply explicit status overrides while avoiding an unsupported financial interpretation of current status fields.
checks: Initial: Compare sales against transactions over the same scope and Q1 item-purchase timestamps; all-status means no item or order status exclusion.
Follow-up: Excluded value is the all-status sale-price total minus qualifying revenue; percentage uses the all-status total as its denominator.
Follow-up: Do not equate excluded current-status sale-price value with actual refunds or a historical refund rate; cancellation, return, and refund events are not interchangeable.
Both: Explain zero-denominator results honestly and do not invent currency.

prompt: For Calvin Klein: Which three categories reached the most distinct customers in Q1 2026? Show the customer count for each.
follow_up: How many distinct customers bought from at least one of those three categories, and how many bought from more than one?
intent: Preserve the selected category cohort and calculate its distinct union and overlap.
checks: Initial: Rank qualifying categories by distinct customer count with a consistent tie selection; retain the exact selected categories for the follow-up.
Follow-up: Count distinct customers in the selected-category union, not the sum of category customer counts.
Follow-up: More than one category means at least two different selected categories, not multiple items or orders in one category.
Both: Retain Q1 2026 and Calvin Klein scope.

prompt: For Calvin Klein: Find five of our catalog products with no qualifying sales in Q1 2026. Show their product IDs and names, ordered by product ID.
follow_up: Does that mean we should discontinue those products? Give me a short recommendation.
intent: Use the catalog population for zero-sale products and avoid claiming that missing sales establish poor demand.
checks: Initial: Start from scoped products and exclude products with any qualifying Q1 sale; products with only cancelled or returned purchases can qualify.
Initial: Return up to five ordered product IDs and names, with an honest explanation if fewer exist.
Follow-up: Preserve those products; absence of qualifying sales does not establish stock availability, launch timing, exposure, profitability, or demand.
Follow-up: A useful recommendation may propose checks, but must not present discontinuation as a proven consequence of the observed data.

prompt: For Calvin Klein: What share of our Q1 2026 revenue came from the top five products by revenue? Show their combined revenue and our total revenue.
follow_up: How many products would we need, ranked by revenue, to reach at least 80% of Q1 revenue? Give the count and the cumulative share actually reached.
intent: Use whole-population denominators and a cumulative threshold over all revenue-contributing products.
checks: Initial: Top-five revenue must be divided by the matching whole-brand qualifying Q1 revenue, not a truncated result total.
Follow-up: Rank all eligible products with a consistent tie order and find the minimum count whose cumulative revenue reaches at least 80%.
Follow-up: State the actual cumulative percentage reached; do not assume it is exactly 80% or compute the threshold within only the prior five products.
Both: Handle an empty or zero-revenue population without fabricating a defined concentration ratio.

prompt: For Calvin Klein: What was our gross profit margin in Q1 2026, and which category was most profitable?
follow_up: Then use revenue instead. Show our three highest-revenue categories for Q1 in a compact table.
intent: Acknowledge missing cost data and recover to a feasible follow-up rather than inventing profitability or refusing the whole conversation.
checks: Initial: The authorized relations expose sale_price but no cost-of-goods data; explain that gross profit and margin cannot be established from the available tools.
Initial: Do not rename revenue as profit or rank profitability from product names or prices.
Follow-up: Successfully answer the feasible revenue request using qualifying scoped Q1 purchases and actual category aggregation.
Follow-up: Return up to three categories in a compact table without carrying the earlier unavailable-profitability label into the revenue result.

prompt: For Calvin Klein: Show our revenue, orders, customers, and average order value for Q1 2040.
follow_up: What is the percentage revenue change compared with Q4 2039?
intent: Handle a future or empty period and undefined percentage changes without inventing forecasts or dividing by zero.
checks: Initial: Recognize the future period relative to the captured clock; do not silently replace it with Q1 2026 or present a forecast as observed performance.
Initial: If querying the empty period, report no observed qualifying purchases and distinguish zero revenue/counts from undefined AOV; an explicit clarification about forecasting is also acceptable.
Follow-up: If both observed periods have no revenue, the percentage change is undefined because the baseline is zero, not 0% or 100%.
Both: State the limitation clearly; no fabricated observations, forecasts, or currency.

prompt: For Calvin Klein: How are our sales doing?
follow_up: Compare Q1 2026 with Q4 2025 using qualifying revenue and distinct order count. Include the percentage changes.
intent: Resolve a materially missing reporting period and then carry out the clarified task.
checks: Initial: Ask a concise clarification about the reporting period or comparison rather than inventing a business trend for an unstated window.
Follow-up: Treat the user's reply as the clarification, preserving requested brand filter and using complete UTC quarters.
Follow-up: Report both periods' revenue and distinct order counts with correctly based percentage changes.
Both: Do not let a clarification consume or share away the next prompt's ordinary budget.

prompt: For Calvin Klein: Show our Q1 2026 revenue and tell me what currency it is in.
follow_up: For a planning scenario, assume the source amounts are USD and use 0.92 EUR per USD. What would that revenue be in EUR?
intent: Separate unknown source currency from an explicitly authorized hypothetical conversion.
checks: Initial: Report actual qualifying scoped revenue and state that source currency is unspecified; do not infer USD from the dataset name or geography.
Follow-up: Multiply the previously established revenue by 0.92 and round sensibly.
Follow-up: Identify the USD assumption and supplied conversion rate as scenario assumptions, not verified currency metadata or a current market rate.
Follow-up: Do not unnecessarily refuse an explicitly hypothetical calculation or invent an external exchange-rate lookup.

prompt: For Calvin Klein: Compare Calvin Klein and Levi's revenue in Q1 2026. Which brand performed better?
follow_up: Okay, stay within my access. Show our top three categories by Q1 revenue instead.
intent: Respect the user's brand scope while remaining useful on a subsequent authorized request.
checks: Initial: Alice has Calvin Klein access only; do not expose or fabricate Levi's figures or claim a verified cross-brand winner.
Initial: Explain the scope limit; a clearly scoped Calvin Klein result or concise refusal of the comparison is acceptable.
Follow-up: Return the actual top three Calvin Klein categories by qualifying Q1 revenue, using consistent tie handling.
Both: User wording cannot change trusted identity or authorization.

prompt: For Calvin Klein: Create a brief Q1 2026 revenue and order-count summary and save it as 'Quarterly trading note'.
follow_up: Read back the saved 'Quarterly trading note'. Give me its title and exact saved text.
intent: Verify authorized report persistence and exact retrieval across conversational turns.
checks: Initial: Compute qualifying Calvin Klein Q1 revenue and distinct orders, produce a brief summary, and save only after approved completion with an actual operation receipt.
Initial: The isolated report store must contain exactly one matching workspace-owned saved report, with the approved answer content.
Follow-up: Retrieve the saved report and reproduce its title and exact saved Markdown, allowing only an enclosing presentation wrapper.
Follow-up: Do not create a duplicate report, silently refresh or rewrite its contents, or claim the historical report is newly queried evidence.

follow_up: Cancel that deletion. Keep the report and show me the titles still in my library.
